The provided UAE PDPL excerpts do not specify a deadline for notifying the supervisory authority or data subjects about a personal data breach.

The retrieved UAE excerpts do not set a deadline for OpCo to notify the Bureau of a personal data breach; Article 13(1)(h) only requires that data subjects be told what actions will be taken in the event of a breach.

UAE telecommunications and consumer protection excerpts do not specify a fixed deadline for a licensee to notify the regulator or affected subscribers after a Subscriber Information breach involving an AI chatbot or vendor change.

The retrieved UAE PDPL excerpts do not impose an explicit personal data breach notification obligation on OpCo as Controller to notify the supervisory authority or affected data subjects after a breach.
The UAE excerpts contain no specific rule requiring security measures for AI chatbots or addressing prompt-injection attacks; only general breach notification duties apply.
The UAE PDPL excerpts do not specify a mandatory deadline or hour figure for notifying the supervisory authority or data subjects of a personal data breach.
No clear owner or approval gate is identified in the retrieved UAE texts for vendor updates to an AI chatbot's data retrieval scope before deployment.
UAE telecom regulation does not explicitly address AI chatbot security controls, prompt injection risks, or cross-border hosting of chatbot data.

The UAE PDPL excerpts provide a data subject right to complain to the Bureau but do not state a specific deadline for a controller to notify the Bureau of a personal data breach, so the timeliness of OpCo's Day 1 notification cannot be assessed against a local statutory deadline.
The UAE PDPL does not specify a breach notification deadline in hours; the implementing regulations necessary for breach notifications have not been issued.
The provided UAE-PDPL excerpts do not impose an explicit duty on OpCo to notify the Bureau or affected data subjects of a personal data breach, nor do they set a deadline for such notification.

The provided UAE text does not identify an owner or deadline for controlling vendor-hosted model configuration and chat logs outside the UAE; the vendor changed the retrieval scope and OpCo learned of the exposure only after about 1,200 sessions.

No single UAE body is identified in the excerpts as lead coordinator for a telecom personal data breach with cross-border hosting, creating overlap between TDRA's telecom consumer-protection oversight and DPA's data-breach role.
The UAE excerpts impose no explicit deadline for OpCo to notify TDRA or submit an incident report after a personal data breach; Article 30 allows requests but states no timeline.
The UAE excerpts do not impose a proactive obligation on licensees to self-report a security incident affecting subscriber personal data; only a regulator-triggered request is visible.

The available UAE PDPL primary text requires breach notification to the Bureau 'within the period' set by the Executive Regulations, but states no hour or day figure, leaving the operational deadline indeterminate in this record.

Multiple institutions are handling the same incident, but the available UAE text names only the Bureau as the recipient of controller breach notification and provides no coordinating owner or information-sharing duty among NOC, REG, CSC, and the Bureau.

The UAE National Cyber Security Policy for Artificial Intelligence requires efficient incident reporting and management for AI security incidents, but the excerpts set no specific deadline for operators or vendors to report an AI chatbot data breach to the Cyber Security Council.

The incident exposed an unclear owner for coordinating AI chatbot breaches between the DPA's personal data breach notification and the Cyber Security Council's national cyber incident response; the strategy envisages cross-agency intelligence sharing but the excerpts do not name a single owner for joint AI vendor incidents.
